newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court allows aid in parochial schools.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court allows aid in parochial schools.

text.p: The Supreme Court, taking the rare step of overturning its own 12-year-old ruling in an important church-state case, held Monday that public school teachers may conduct remedial classes at parochial schools.
The high court by a 5-4 vote ruled that allowing public school teachers into private schools for remedial classes does not violate the constitutional requirement of separation of church and state.

The decision was a victory for the Clinton administration, which argued that the 1985 Supreme Court ruling made it more difficult and costly to provide remedial educational and counselling services to low-income students in private schools.

The federal government, New York City and parents of a group of parochial school children had asked the justices to reopen the long-running legal dispute and allow public school teachers to go into the private schools.

Justice Sandra Day O'Connor said for the conservative court majority that the programme passes constitutional scrutiny, noting that New York City had sufficient safeguards to prevent improper church-state entanglement.

She declared that the Supreme Court's 1985 ruling barring public school teachers from offering remedial classes in church schools, and part of a decision in a similar case that same year, were "no longer good law."

O'Connor said the New York City programme does not result in government indoctrination or define its recipients by reference to religion and cannot be viewed as a government endorsement of religion. "We therefore hold that a federally funded programme providing supplemental, remedial instruction to disadvantaged children on a neutral basis is not invalid."
The court's most liberal members dissented, with Justice David Souter charging that the ruling authorises "direct state aid to religious institutions on an unparalleled scale."

Under the majority's logic, Souter wrote, state governments will be free next "to assume, or assume payment for, the entire cost of instruction provided in any ostensibly secular subject in any religious school."
The 1985 ruling did not ban teachers from helping parochial school students but the help had to be offered in public schools, in mobile classrooms, by computer or even on school buses.
The high court has become more conservative over the past 12 years, lowering the wall of separation between church and state and casting strong doubt about whether the 1985 ruling would survive.
The Justice Department argued that hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent needlessly by public school systems nationwide to comply with the 1985 decision, imposing a major financial burden.

The Education Department under the Clinton administration took the same position as the Republican Reagan administration in arguing that public school teachers should be allowed to conduct the classes at religious schools.
